title: Gap Detection by Section and Perturbation Type
note: Share of the 12 runs (4 models × 3 conditions) that found each gap, split by the section of the reference Code of Conduct it belongs to and by how it was injected. Columns run hardest to easiest. Cells backed by fewer than three gold gaps are left uncoloured rather than shown as noise.
alt: Six by ten matrix of detection rates. Rows are reference sections, columns are perturbation types ordered hardest to easiest. Darker means more often detected.
caption: Read down a column to separate topic from perturbation type: for modality edits the rate falls from 0.81 in Human rights to 0.56 in Verification, and the same ordering holds for scope and omission. Reweighting every section to the corpus-wide perturbation mix narrows the spread only from 0.227 to 0.203.

title: Cost of Conditions A + BT against Pooled Gap Recall
note: Pooled across conditions A (raw text) and BT (raw text + induced schema), 150 documents each. Cost is billed spend for those 300 calls.
alt: Scatter plot of four language models, cost in dollars on the vertical axis against pooled gap recall on the horizontal axis, connected in order of increasing recall.
caption: Models ordered left to right by recall. The two open models cluster cheaply at low recall; Claude Sonnet 5 climbs to $37.21, and GPT-5.6-terra then reaches higher recall for $9.63.

title: Component-Level Comparison at the Frame Layer
note: Why the schema carries a frame layer at all. Read left to right: topic-level alignment can only ask whether both documents cover Reporting Violations, and both do, so the node is atomic and an omission inside it is invisible. The FrameNet frame attached to that node supplies the checklist — Informer, Authorities, Behavior — from an external inventory rather than from the model's own reading, and binding values to those elements turns the comparison into three checkable slots.
alt: Three panels. (a) A reference code and a candidate code both attach to the same taxonomy node, Reporting Violations, so a coverage comparison records the topic as present in both. (b) The node carries the FrameNet frame Reporting, whose core frame elements Informer, Authorities and Behavior state what a complete provision must specify. (c) Binding values to those elements shows the candidate narrows Informer from any employee or third party to permanent employees only, and omits the Authorities channel, while Behavior matches — two gaps where topic alignment found none.
caption: Example of component-level comparison for the Reporting Violations topic (§4.6): frame-element binding reveals a narrowed reporter scope and an omitted reporting channel that topic-level alignment alone would miss.

title: Taxonomy and Schema, by Example
note: What the two layers look like, taken from the schema induced over the reference Code of Conduct. Concepts form one rooted tree; each concept carries FrameNet frames whose core elements are the slots a complete provision would fill.
alt: Two panels. (a) The topic taxonomy: one path seven levels deep from the root, Ethical Principles and Training, down to Reporting of Ethical Violations, with the number of sibling concepts collapsed at each level; the full taxonomy holds 107 concepts and reaches depth 8. (b) The schema on that concept: it carries the FrameNet frame Reporting, whose four core elements are Informer, Wrongdoer, Authorities and Behavior. Three are bound to values from the document, each backed by a verbatim quote; Wrongdoer is left unfilled.
caption: Example taxonomy and schema (§4.4). The tree on the left is the induced taxonomy, one path of it; the stack on the right is what hangs off a single concept. Three of the four core slots are filled and Wrongdoer is not — an omission visible only because the frame named the slot in advance.

title: From PDF to DocItem Tree
note: Docling's layout model assigns each page region a type; the reading-order stream it emits is then resolved into the nested DocItem tree the pipeline consumes.
alt: Diagram: a page mockup with typed layout regions (H, Tx, DI) is flattened into a reading-order stream by Docling, then resolved by heading-hierarchy resolution and chunking into a nested DocItem tree rooted at #/body.
caption: From PDF to DocItem tree, illustrated on a document in our corpus. (a) Docling's layout model assigns each page region a type (H = section header, Tx = text, DI = document index / table); a six-element excerpt is shown. (b) The same elements as Docling emits them: a flat, ordered stream. (c) doc_chunks_to_doc_items (§4.1) resolves heading levels into the nested tree the pipeline consumes, shown here in full for this document's top level, not restricted to the (a)–(b) excerpt. The DOCUMENT_INDEX node under “Table of Contents” is retained in the tree but excluded from section text used downstream (§4.1); nested subsections (e.g., “3.1”) and their list items are resolved into proper descendants rather than a flat sequence.

title: LLM-guided Placement Search
note: LLM-guided placement of a summarized section s into the shared taxonomy T. Search recurses down one branch at a time, deciding at each node whether to stop, match, or explore further; Place arbitrates when more than one branch reports back.

lines.text: return ⟨v, a, U⟩ ∥ Search(T, last(U), s)
